name: memcpy_benchmark (memcpy_avx256 and memcpy_movsb in NASM)
baseline: glibc memcpy as linked by the system cc (version not stated)
workload: One 128 MiB memcpy from a freshly malloc'd and memset source into a freshly malloc'd destination, repeated 10 times and timed with gettimeofday; compares libc memcpy, AVX2 loop, AVX-512 loop and rep movsb.
claimed_speedup: result.txt Avg seconds: Xeon Platinum 8269CY libc 0.3853, AVX 0.2987, AVX-512 0.3150, rep movsb 0.3333 (AVX about 1.29x vs libc, derived from page data); AMD A8-6410 libc 0.6221, AVX 0.4967, rep movsb 0.4970 (about 1.25x, derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Single-size, large-buffer routines only (x86-64 Linux, NASM). The AVX/AVX-512 variants need the matching CPU features; rep movsb needs ERMS for good behaviour. Public-domain dedication, no patent grant. No handling shown for small or overlapping copies (memcpy only).
caveats: Only one 128 MiB size is measured, so small-copy behaviour (where glibc is strongest) is not covered. The timed region includes first-touch page faults on the freshly malloc'd destination, which dilutes and may distort the ratios. The loop runs 11 iterations but divides the total by 10 for 'Avg' (same bias for every variant). Compiler and glibc versions are not recorded. Gains of 25-29% on large copies are plausible non-temporal and wide-store effects, not a general memcpy win.

name: FastMemcpy
baseline: memcpy from the toolchain C runtime (gcc 4.9 or MSVC 2012; platform and libc not stated)
workload: Copy of 32 B to 8 MiB buffers (aligned and unaligned source/destination combinations, many repetitions) plus a random-size access run, memcpy_fast versus memcpy, SSE2 or AVX builds.
claimed_speedup: README: '50% speedup in avg. vs traditional memcpy in msvc 2012 or gcc 4.9'. gcc 4.9 rows (memcpy_fast vs memcpy, ms): 32 B x16777216 aligned 81 vs 281; 512 B aligned 124 vs 242; 8192 B aligned 55 vs 70; 4 MiB aligned 263 vs 398; random access 487 vs 1000. Slower case: 1 MiB aligned 181 vs 165.
tradeoffs: Header-style C implementation: jump table for small sizes, SSE2/AVX vector copy for medium, prefetch plus non-temporal stores (movntdq) for huge sizes. README says it only handles the aligned huge-copy case from the AMD block-prefetch paper and the user must handle other cases. SSE2 or AVX build must match the target CPU.
caveats: CPU model is not stated, gcc 4.9 and MSVC 2012 are very old, and the baseline libc/OS is not identified, so the 3x small-copy wins may reflect an old, slow memcpy rather than a current glibc with ifunc dispatch. Numbers are single-run and there are no modern glibc/musl comparisons. The README's 'over 50% in average' is not backed by a computed figure, and the 1 MiB aligned row shows memcpy_fast losing.

workload: Runtime of code compiled with and without the Minotaur LLVM pass: SPEC CPU 2017, the GMP benchmark suite and LibYUV.
claimed_speedup: OOPSLA 2024 paper, per WebSearch result text only (paper not opened): SPEC CPU 2017 mean speedup 1.5% on Intel (1.2% on AMD) with a maximum of 4.5% on 638.imagick; GMP benchmark suite mean 7.3% with a maximum of 13% on an Intel Cascade Lake processor; LibYUV geomean 1.029x on AMD Zen 3.
hardware: Intel Cascade Lake (GMP), AMD Zen 3 (LibYUV); other CPUs per paper not confirmed
tradeoffs: Runs as an LLVM opt pass or via minotaur-cc / minotaur-c++ wrappers; needs a patched, RTTI- and EH-enabled LLVM build, Alive2, Z3 and Redis (offline cache mode), which makes the build heavy. Synthesis time adds to compile time.
caveats: All numbers come from search-result text of the paper (arxiv 2306.00229, blocked in this environment) and have not been checked on the paper itself; the repo README has no performance numbers and no evaluation directory was seen. Gains on SPEC are small (1.2-1.5% mean). Peer review (OOPSLA 2024) taken from a SPLASH 2024 programme page snippet. It is an LLVM IR superoptimizer, so only loosely 'assembly tooling'.
found_via: WebSearch 'superoptimizer outperforms gcc -O3 ...' and 'Minotaur SIMD-oriented superoptimizer LLVM evaluation speedup SPEC CPU 2017 geomean results'; opened github.com/minotaur-toolkit/minotaur

name: STOKE
baseline: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 compiled x86-64 code (output quality); expert hand-written assembly for some kernels; Google Native Client's shipped libc string functions in the 2017 paper
workload: Runtime of superoptimized loop-free x86-64 kernels (OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication, Hacker's Delight, SAXPY, linked-list traversal) starting from llvm -O0 code, and 13 libc string functions from NaCl newlib.
claimed_speedup: ASPLOS 2013 paper (PDF opened): the Montgomery multiplication kernel from OpenSSL's big-number library is 16 lines shorter and 1.6x faster than gcc -O3 output and slightly faster than expert handwritten assembly; across the benchmark kernels STOKE matches gcc -O3 and icc -O3 starting from llvm -O0 and in several cases exceeds both. ASPLOS 2017 paper (PDF opened): 'median and average speedup of 25% over the libraries shipped by Google' for 13 libc string functions with formal verification. README tutorial: popcount drops from about 1.05 s to about 0.13 s versus a g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline build.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 baselines (versions not stated in the extracted paper text); gcc-4.9 used in the 2017 paper's translation mode; README tutorial uses g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline
hardware: ASPLOS 2013: synthesis and optimization on a cluster of 40 dual-core 1.8 GHz AMD Opterons (machine used for the runtime speedups not identified in the extracted text); ASPLOS 2017: machines with two Intel Xeon E5-2667v2 3.3 GHz processors and 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: x86-64 only and Intel-microarchitecture oriented. Needs test cases plus bounded or SMT-based equivalence checking, search budgets of tens of minutes per kernel on a cluster, and works best on short loop-free sequences. README: 'STOKE isn't production ready' and 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it says it is 'not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code'.
caveats: Speedups are on hand-picked small kernels, and the ASPLOS 2013 Figure 11 reports speedup over llvm -O0 with STOKE 'comparable' to gcc -O3 and icc -O3 on many kernels, not always faster. The 2017 baseline is Google's shipped NaCl libc code (already constrained by SFI alignment rules), not a plain gcc -O3 build. A 2022 TU Delft bachelor thesis, seen only as a WebSearch snippet (not opened), reports that STOKE often fails to match gcc -O3 and struggles with loops. Not a benchmark of assemble time. Same repo holds both papers (docs/papers/asplos13.pdf, asplos17.pdf, cacm16.pdf and others).
